corrected_value.title: The causal effects of extraversion on positive affect and neuroticism on negative affect: Manipulating state extraversion and state neuroticism in an experimental approach
corrected_value.title_o: The causal effects of extraversion on positive affect and neuroticism on negative affect: Manipulating state extraversion and state neuroticism in an experimental approach
corrected_value.evidence_quote: Although possible, two studies have assessed negative affect under similar circumstances and have failed to find the state by trait interaction that would suggest a mood cost for acting counterdispositionally (McNiel & Fleeson, 2006; McNiel et al., 2010). On the other hand, one of these samples was small (n⫽45) and both employed a within-subject design that could promote demand or carryover effects. In fact, the studies did find significant order effects and some inconsistent trait and acting condition effects on negative affect. So although there was not a significant interaction suggesting an affective cost, the full mood consequences of acting more or less extraverted require some clarification, particularly with regard to negative affect. Therefore, our studies include between-subjects manipulations, larger sample sizes, and measures of both positive and negative affect to better assess any possible distress that might accompany counterdispositional behavior.
corrected_value.outcome_quote: Results replicated and extended past findings suggesting that acting extraverted produces hedonic benefits regardless of disposition. Positive affect increased and negative affect did not, even for participants acting out of character.

prior_decisions.quote: We predicted that Fleeson et al.’s (2002) core findings would replicate. That is, our participants would be able to act as we instructed them, and acting extraverted would cause positive affect, regardless of disposition. Analyses also tested the idea that acting counterdispositionally can lead to increased negative affect. However, given hints from past research, we did not anticipate large negative affective consequences for acting out of character.
prior_decisions.reason: McNiel and Fleeson (2006) is cited only in the introduction as background literature providing prior context on negative affect and state extraversion; the experiments are explicitly framed as a replication and extension of Fleeson et al. (2002) and never evaluate or compare results against McNiel and Fleeson (2006) as a replication target.

scope_review.parent_objection: The first review excludes McNiel&Fleeson2006 and McNiel/Lowman/Fleeson2010 as background. Source inspection shows a specific published finding:two studies assessed negative affect and failed to find the state-by-trait interaction suggesting a mood cost;the paper criticizes their small sample/within-subject designs and says the full mood consequences require clarification. Its own two studies deliberately test the same counterdispositional negative-affect interaction with new participants and a changed design,reporting no negative-affect cost. The codebook decides actual retesting,not whether authors call it an extension relative to Fleeson2002. Determine if each prior negative-affect study is genuinely re-tested or only motivates a different empirical claim. Changed design and an extension label alone cannot exclude a conceptual replication. Account for closest-chain rule from actual citation/design relationship rather than assuming every cited paper is a target. If insufficient,retain uncertainty. Fleeson2002successful outcome remains accepted. This is the second and final call,including mechanical retries.
